description: COG and STAC without leaving the dashboard: DuckDB finds the scene in the catalogue, TiTiler serves it as tiles and measures it, and kepler draws it as a raster.

options.content:
# Cloud-native raster

One query discovers the scene and the map draws it. There is no ETL and no download: DuckDB asks Sentinel-2's STAC catalogue which image covers Cuenca inside the dashboard's range, gets back **one row** with the link to the COG, and the panel hands it to TiTiler, which serves the tiles by reading the remote file over byte ranges. That row carries more than the link: the gauge beside the table reads the scene's **cloud cover** straight out of the catalogue, a number that costs no pixels at all.

The same server also knows how to **measure** what it serves, so the two panels below get numbers out of the raster without bringing a single pixel into the browser: the mean of the red band over an area, and the value of the pixel wherever you click on the map.

| Piece | Who provides it |
|---|---|
| Catalogue | `earth-search.aws.element84.com`, public and unauthenticated |
| Search | DuckDB with the `http_client` extension, parameterised by the range |
| Tiles and statistics | the compose file's `titiler` container |
| Drawing | `RasterTileLayer`, which kepler already ships |

**Move the date range**: the scene and the numbers change, the viewport does not. **Cloud cover ≤** sets how much cloud is tolerable — 60 % to begin with, which over the equatorial Andes is a permissive cut. If no image in the period comes in under it, the query returns nothing and there is no raster to draw.

**The two panels below ask nothing over HTTP.** The zonal statistic is computed inside DuckDB, joining the raster to the table of zones — four zones or four thousand, one query. And the NDVI is computed in SQL and written as a COG, which TiTiler serves exactly like a remote scene:

```sql
COPY (
  SELECT r.geometry,
         -- NDVI (-0.2 .. 0.9) stretched over the integer's range.
         RT_Cube2TypeUInt16(((n.databand_1 - r.databand_1) / (n.databand_1 + r.databand_1)
                             + 0.2) / 1.1 * 65535.0) AS ndvi
  FROM RT_Read('/testdata/raster/cuenca-b04.tif') r
  JOIN RT_Read('/testdata/raster/cuenca-b08.tif') n ON r.id = n.id)
TO '/derived/ndvi-cuenca-u16.tif'
WITH (FORMAT RASTER, DRIVER 'COG', SRS 'EPSG:4326',
      DATABAND_COLUMNS ['ndvi'], CREATION_OPTIONS ('COMPRESS=DEFLATE'));
```

That query is **not** in any panel, and that is deliberate: it writes a file, and a dashboard refreshing every 30 s must not redo a computation each time. It is run once — from Explore, against the DuckDB datasource — and the panels read what is already there. If the NDVI panel comes up empty, nobody has run it yet.

**The integer is not a detail**: kepler will not draw a `float32` raster (the layer is simply missing, with nothing said) and `uint8` comes out as a flat sheet of colour. `uint16` is what works.

panels.description: The same query that feeds the map. Here it is raw, as the panel receives it: one row, with the raster_url column the plugin detects by name.

targets.rawSql:
WITH resp AS (
  SELECT http_get(
    'https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1/search'
    || '?collections=sentinel-2-l2a'
    || '&bbox=-79.10,-3.05,-78.90,-2.85'
    || '&datetime=' || $__timeFrom() || '/' || $__timeTo()
    || '&limit=100'
  ) AS r
),
features AS (
  SELECT unnest(json_extract(r->>'body', '$.features[*]')) AS f FROM resp
)
SELECT
  f->>'id'                                     AS scene_id,
  (f->'properties'->>'datetime')::TIMESTAMP    AS acquired,
  (f->'properties'->>'eo:cloud_cover')::DOUBLE AS cloud_cover,
  f->'assets'->'visual'->>'href'               AS raster_url
FROM features
WHERE (f->'properties'->>'eo:cloud_cover')::DOUBLE <= CAST($cloud AS DOUBLE)
ORDER BY acquired DESC
LIMIT 1

panels.title: The scene chosen for the current range

panels.description:
How much of the scene beside it is cloud, straight from the catalogue: STAC carries `eo:cloud_cover` as a property of every item, so the number costs no pixels — it arrives with the search that picked the image.

It is a **scene-level** figure, measured over the whole Sentinel-2 granule rather than over the box this dashboard looks at. Cuenca sits in a corner of the tile, so a cloudy granule can still be clear here, and a clear one can be socked in.

The needle can never pass the cut set in **Cloud cover ≤**, because anything above it is never chosen — so it also shows how much room the scene had. The coloured bands, at 25 %, 50 % and 60 %, are fixed marks and do not follow the selector: Grafana's thresholds take numbers, not variables.

targets.rawSql:
WITH resp AS (
  SELECT http_get(
    'https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1/search'
    || '?collections=sentinel-2-l2a'
    || '&bbox=-79.10,-3.05,-78.90,-2.85'
    || '&datetime=' || $__timeFrom() || '/' || $__timeTo()
    || '&limit=100'
  ) AS r
),
features AS (
  SELECT unnest(json_extract(r->>'body', '$.features[*]')) AS f FROM resp
)
SELECT
  (f->'properties'->>'eo:cloud_cover')::DOUBLE AS cloud_cover
FROM features
WHERE (f->'properties'->>'eo:cloud_cover')::DOUBLE <= CAST($cloud AS DOUBLE)
ORDER BY (f->'properties'->>'datetime')::TIMESTAMP DESC
LIMIT 1

panels.description: A zonal statistic computed by TiTiler: it clips the red band with the polygon and returns the summary. One HTTP request, zero pixels in the browser.
panels.title: Mean red reflectance · Cuenca area

panels.description: RT_CubeClip + RT_CubeStats_Agg with GROUP BY: one row per zone, joined to the population already living in the table. Four zones or four thousand, it is the same query.

targets.rawSql:
-- Estadística zonal dentro de la base de datos: el ráster se une a tus
-- propias tablas en SQL, en una sola consulta, en vez de una petición HTTP
-- por zona. Es lo que un servidor de teselas no puede hacer.
LOAD raster; LOAD spatial;
WITH zonas AS (
  SELECT name, population, geometry AS geom
  FROM read_parquet('/testdata/cuenca-zones.parquet')
),
teselas AS (
  SELECT geometry, tile_x, tile_y, metadata, databand_1 AS band
  FROM RT_Read('/testdata/raster/cuenca-b04.tif')
),
recortes AS (
  -- El recorte rellena con 0 fuera del polígono; declararlo nodata es lo que
  -- impide que ese relleno entre en la media.
  SELECT z.name, z.population,
         RT_CubeSetNoData(RT_CubeClip(t.band, t.tile_x, t.tile_y, t.metadata, z.geom, 0.0), 0.0) AS cube
  FROM teselas t JOIN zonas z ON ST_Intersects(t.geometry, z.geom)
)
SELECT name AS zona,
       round((RT_CubeStats_Agg(cube, 0)).mean, 1)   AS reflectancia_media,
       (RT_CubeStats_Agg(cube, 0)).valid_count      AS pixeles,
       (RT_CubeStats_Agg(cube, 0)).minimum          AS minimo,
       (RT_CubeStats_Agg(cube, 0)).maximum          AS maximo,
       population                                   AS poblacion
FROM recortes
GROUP BY name, population
ORDER BY reflectancia_media DESC

panels.title: Zonal statistics computed in DuckDB

panels.description:
NDVI computed in SQL from two bands and written as a COG; TiTiler serves it and kepler draws it. The panel cannot tell this raster from a remote scene.

The ramp is set to Greens on purpose. kepler's default (Cfastie) was built for drone NDVI and steps through unrelated colours, so a continuous index comes out as confetti — the index is monotonic and its ramp has to be too.

targets.rawSql:
-- El COG que escribió la consulta de arriba. Para el panel esto es una URL
-- como cualquier otra: la misma tubería que dibuja una escena de Sentinel.
SELECT file AS raster_url FROM glob('/derived/ndvi-*.tif') ORDER BY file LIMIT 1

list.description: The most cloud a scene may carry and still be chosen. It is the catalogue's own `eo:cloud_cover`, measured over the whole Sentinel-2 granule rather than over Cuenca, so it is a coarse cut: 60 % is the default because over the equatorial Andes a stricter one often leaves the range with no image at all.
list.label: Cloud cover ≤
list.name: cloud

list.description: The red band of the same scene the map draws, re-resolved whenever the range changes.
list.label: Red band of the scene
list.name: cog
list.query:
WITH resp AS (
  SELECT http_get(
    'https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1/search'
    || '?collections=sentinel-2-l2a'
    || '&bbox=-79.10,-3.05,-78.90,-2.85'
    || '&datetime=' || $__timeFrom() || '/' || $__timeTo()
    || '&limit=100'
  ) AS r
),
features AS (
  SELECT unnest(json_extract(r->>'body', '$.features[*]')) AS f FROM resp
)
SELECT f->'assets'->'red'->>'href'
FROM features
-- Ojo: dentro de una query de VARIABLE Grafana no entrecomilla, así que las
-- comillas de '${cloud}' van a mano. En los paneles es al revés: $cloud llega
-- ya entrecomillado y el CAST es el que lo devuelve a número.
WHERE (f->'properties'->>'eo:cloud_cover')::DOUBLE <= CAST('${cloud}' AS DOUBLE)
ORDER BY (f->'properties'->>'datetime')::TIMESTAMP DESC
LIMIT 1
